explanations.answer: How He got such learning without studying
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The Jews ask, “How did this man attain such learning without having studied?” (John 7:15) I think they were looking around for the diploma on the wall. I'd have the same trouble, because my paperwork would say "found in a junk drawer."

explanations.answer: Why He waited so long to come and teach
explanations.explanation: Nobody in the passage asks about timing. Jesus went up about halfway through the feast, and the Jews were amazed at His teaching. What they ask is how He got such learning without having studied. Nobody taps a watch and says "What took You?"

explanations.answer: Who gave Him permission to teach right here
explanations.explanation: Close, but that's not the question they ask. Jesus goes up to the temple courts and begins to teach, and the Jews are amazed. Their question is about His learning: how did He get it without having studied? Nobody asks to see a badge.

explanations.answer: From the One who sent Him
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus replies, “My teaching is not My own.” Then He says, “It comes from Him who sent Me.” The Jews asked about His schooling, and He points past every classroom to the One who sent Him.

Jesus doesn't name any teacher in Jerusalem. The Jews wondered how He learned so much without having studied. He answers, “My teaching is not My own,” and says it comes from Him who sent Him. That's a bigger source than any teacher in the city.

explanations.answer: From years of reading the Scriptures
explanations.explanation: That would be a fair guess, but Jesus doesn't give a study plan. The Jews were amazed that He had such learning without having studied. He tells them, “My teaching is not My own.” It comes from Him who sent Him.

explanations.answer: Anyone who desires to do God's will
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Jesus says, “If anyone desires to do His will, he will know whether My teaching is from God or whether I speak on My own.” It's about the desire, not the résumé. Anyone can show up with that.

explanations.answer: Anyone who has studied the law
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't tie it to studying. The Jews were wondering about His learning, but His answer is about what a person wants. He says, “If anyone desires to do His will, he will know…” So the door is open to anyone, not just the people with the most study hours.

explanations.answer: Anyone who has seen His miracles
explanations.explanation: Seeing a miracle isn't what He names here. Jesus says, “If anyone desires to do His will, he will know whether My teaching is from God or whether I speak on My own.” The key is the desire to do God's will. That's something any person can bring with them.

You got it, baker. Jesus says, “He who speaks on his own authority seeks his own glory.” That's the person who narrates his own highlight reel. Then Jesus turns it around and talks about the one who seeks the glory of the One who sent Him.

Jesus doesn't say that about this person. He says, “He who speaks on his own authority seeks his own glory.” That's the self-promoter. The one who seeks the glory of the One who sent Him is a different person.

That one belongs to the other person in the verse. Jesus says the one who speaks on his own authority seeks his own glory. Then He says the one who seeks the glory of the One who sent Him is “a man of truth.” Two different people, and the choice is easy to mix up.

explanations.answer: Why are you trying to kill Me
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. After He says that none of them keeps the law of Moses, Jesus asks, “Why are you trying to kill Me?” (John 7:19) John had already told us the Jews in Judea were looking for a way to kill Him (John 7:1). This is a heavy moment, and Jesus says it straight out.

explanations.answer: Why do you doubt My teaching
explanations.explanation: He doesn't ask about doubt. Right after saying that not one of them keeps the law, Jesus asks, “Why are you trying to kill Me?” That's a much sharper question. It puts the real problem right out in the open.

explanations.answer: Why did you come to this feast
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't ask about why they came. He has just said not one of them keeps the law of Moses. Then He asks, “Why are you trying to kill Me?” It's a heavy question, and He says it plainly.
The crowd doesn't admit anything. They answer, “You have a demon.” Then they ask, “Who is trying to kill You?” So instead of owning it, they act like they've never heard of it.
That's right, baker. The crowd doesn't admit it. They say, “You have a demon,” and then ask, “Who is trying to kill You?” That's a long way from "yes, it's us."
Yes, baker. Jesus says circumcision is “not that it is from Moses, but from the patriarchs.” Moses was Israel's leader, and he gave them the law. The practice reaches back even before him.

Jesus says the opposite. Moses, Israel's leader, gave them circumcision, but Jesus adds that it is “not that it is from Moses, but from the patriarchs.” So He does point back past Moses. It's a quick side note in the middle of His point.

Yes, friend. Jesus asks, “…why are you angry with Me for making the whole man well on the Sabbath?” A boy can be circumcised on the Sabbath, and Jesus makes the whole man well on that same day. He asks them to look at the two side by side.

Nothing in the verse is about being made wise. Jesus asks why they are angry with Him “for making the whole man well on the Sabbath.” It's about healing a whole person. Wise sounds nice, but it isn't what He says.
Calm is the one thing missing from that scene. Jesus asks why they are angry with Him “for making the whole man well on the Sabbath.” The word is well, as in healed. Nobody in that crowd sounds calm.
That's the word, baker. Jesus says, “Stop judging by outward appearances, and start judging justly.” Looks can fool anybody. Judging justly means looking deeper.
Speed isn't what Jesus is after. He says, “Stop judging by outward appearances, and start judging justly.” A fast judgment can still go by looks. He asks for judging that is just.
Jesus doesn't ask for harsh judging. He says, “Stop judging by outward appearances, and start judging justly.” The goal is fairness, not toughness. It's a different thing entirely.

That's right, friend. Some people of Jerusalem say, “Yet here He is, speaking publicly, and they are not saying anything to Him.” They were thinking it was strange. Then they ask if the rulers have truly recognized that this is the Christ.

They do notice it. The people of Jerusalem say, “Yet here He is, speaking publicly, and they are not saying anything to Him.” It puzzles them enough that they wonder whether the rulers have truly recognized that this is the Christ. Nobody had to point it out to them.

explanations.answer: No one will know where the Christ is from
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The people say, “But we know where this man is from. When the Christ comes, no one will know where He is from.” In their minds, knowing where Jesus is from counts against Him. They talk themselves right out of it.

explanations.answer: The Christ will come from the line of priests
explanations.explanation: Priests don't come up in their reasoning. They say, “When the Christ comes, no one will know where He is from.” Since they know where Jesus is from, they doubt it. Nothing there is about a line of priests.

explanations.answer: The Christ will grow up in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: They don't say that. Their reasoning is, “When the Christ comes, no one will know where He is from.” They know where Jesus is from, so that's their doubt. Jerusalem isn't part of the argument.

Jesus says the opposite. He tells them, “You know Me, and you know where I am from.” Then He says of the One who sent Him, “You do not know Him.” That's a lot to take in while standing in the temple courts.

That's right, baker. Jesus says of the One who sent Him, “You do not know Him, but I know Him, because I am from Him and He sent Me.” They know where Jesus is from, but they don't know the One who sent Him.

explanations.answer: His hour had not yet come
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. They try to seize Him, but no one lays a hand on Him “because His hour had not yet come.” The text gives that as the reason. Nobody was moving until then.

explanations.answer: The priests told them to wait
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. It says no one laid a hand on Jesus “because His hour had not yet come.” The chief priests do show up later, when they send officers to arrest Him with the Pharisees (John 7:32). That isn't why these people held back.

explanations.answer: His disciples stood in the way
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention the disciples here. It says no one laid a hand on Jesus “because His hour had not yet come.” That's the whole reason it gives. No one needed to block the door.

Yes, baker. Many in the crowd believe in Him and say, “When the Christ comes, will He perform more signs than this man?” They look at what Jesus has done and ask who could do more. That's the crowd's reasoning, and it leads them to believe.

They aren't comparing sermons. The crowd asks, “When the Christ comes, will He perform more signs than this man?” It's about signs, the things Jesus has done. Teaching is going on, but that isn't what they count.
Sacrifices aren't in that question. The crowd says, “When the Christ comes, will He perform more signs than this man?” The word is signs. They're counting what Jesus has done.
Yes, friend. The Pharisees and the chief priests send officers to arrest Him. That's the text's own wording. The whispering in the crowd gets a response from the leaders.

explanations.answer: Ask Jesus to teach them more
explanations.explanation: That's not what they do. When the Pharisees hear the crowd whispering, they and the chief priests send officers to arrest Jesus. They bring officers, not questions. Not exactly a student's move.

explanations.answer: Order the crowd to go home
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say they send anyone home. When the Pharisees hear the whispering, they and the chief priests send officers to arrest Jesus. The target is Jesus, not the crowd.
Jesus says the opposite. He tells them, “You will look for Me, but you will not find Me.” He adds, “…where I am, you cannot come.” I think that's why they're confused by it.
That's right, baker. Jesus says, “You will look for Me, but you will not find Me.” He also says, “…where I am, you cannot come.” The looking is in there, but the finding is not.

explanations.answer: To the Jews scattered among the Greeks
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The Jews ask, “Will He go where the Jews are dispersed among the Greeks, and teach the Greeks?” That's their guess, and it's only a guess. Nobody has told them where He means.

explanations.answer: Back up north to the towns of Galilee
explanations.explanation: Galilee isn't part of their guess. They ask, “Will He go where the Jews are dispersed among the Greeks, and teach the Greeks?” That's where their minds go. It's a long way off.

explanations.answer: Out into the wilderness near the Jordan
explanations.explanation: They don't mention the wilderness. Their guess is, “Will He go where the Jews are dispersed among the Greeks, and teach the Greeks?” That's the place they come up with. The Jordan never comes up.
